brief.question: What were the main debates in the Australian parliament in 2025, and what positions did members and parties take? Debates that year included The housing crisis, Cost of living, The under-16 social media ban and The energy transition.
brief.answer:
In 2025, the Australian parliament was dominated by debates over the cost-of-living and housing crises. Opposition members, including the Liberal and National parties, repeatedly argued that Australians were not better off under the Labor government, citing a "cost-of-living crisis, a housing crisis and an energy bill crisis." They pointed to specific figures, such as housing construction falling from 250,000 per year to insufficient levels after 1.2 million immigrants arrived in two years, farm energy bills doubling from $1,200 to over $2,400, and 27,000 business insolvencies. They also highlighted falling GP bulk-billing rates in their electorates, with one member noting a drop from 93 per cent in 2019 to as low as 79 per cent under Labor, and another from 79 per cent to 69 per cent. Government speakers defended their record, citing 18 months of real wage growth, energy bill relief of $150, and solar battery discounts, while accusing the opposition of using migrants as scapegoats for housing crises and opposing measures like student debt cuts and cheaper medicines.

The government also advanced specific legislative responses. The Help to Buy (Commonwealth Powers) Bill 2025 was supported as a solution to the housing crisis, with criticism directed at opposition members for blocking innovative housing policies. A separate debate concerned the Housing Australia Investment Mandate Amendment (Delivering on Our 2025 Election Commitment) Direction 2025, which was moved to take note of, with debate adjourned. On social media, the parliament debated the Albanese government's ban on social media for under-16s, set to take effect from 10 December 2025. The government argued this world-leading action would protect young Australians from pressures and risks, giving them three more years to build resilience, with the ban applying to Australian residents and including reporting and appeals mechanisms. Opposition members, however, framed the broader context as one of crisis, with one speaker noting that cost of living had become the No. 1 issue in Mission Australia's annual youth survey for the first time in November 2024, with the percentage of young people worrying about it more than doubling in two years.
